stances.claim: The Court 'went beyond two sets of normal rules' -- discarding the unsigned-resolution '1-2-3 rule' and the no-factual-review default -- to conduct an exhaustive factual review and overturn the unanimous lower-tribunal finding that Lazada riders were independent contractors.
stances.rhetorical_move: Procedural-departure framing: identifies the deviation from default appellate behavior as itself the activist signal.

stances.claim: Under the four-fold test (selection/engagement, wages, dismissal power, control), with control as 'the most significant factor,' Lazada riders are regular employees because Lazada failed to discharge its burden of proving otherwise.
stances.rhetorical_move: Doctrinal exposition of the operative test before applying it to the gig-economy facts.
stances.confidence: very high -- direct application of binding doctrine

stances.claim: The riders cannot qualify as independent contractors because they neither carried on a 'distinct and independent business' nor possessed the 'unique skills and talents' that distinguish the small class of genuinely independent service providers (the columnist, the basketball referee, the masiador/sentenciador in cockfighting).
stances.rhetorical_move: Negative-pattern matching: contrasts the rider against the canonical exception class.

stances.claim: The Court's closing paragraph -- 'When a person has no property, his job may possibly be his only possession or means of livelihood. Therefore, he should be protected against any arbitrary deprivation of his job' -- is 'reminiscent of my own philosophy of liberty and prosperity under the rule of law.'
stances.rhetorical_move: Personal-philosophical claim of lineage: Court echoes Panganiban's own framework.

notable_anecdotes.description: The procedural normalcy violated in three ways: (1) the 1-2-3 rule -- when the CA affirms NLRC and LA, the SC normally dismisses via unsigned resolution finding 'no reversible error'; (2) the no-factual-review default -- the SC normally reviews only errors of law because lower tribunals are better equipped to find facts; and (3) the grave-abuse threshold for certiorari review of NLRC -- 'arbitrary or despotic manner by reason of passion or personal hostility... so patent and gross as to amount to an evasion of positive duty.'
notable_anecdotes.purpose: Itemizes the procedural defaults the Court bypassed, making the activist deviation legible.

notable_anecdotes.description: The canonical 'unique skills and talents' exception class enumerated by the Court: 'a columnist who was hired because of her talent, skill, experience, and feminist standpoint, a basketball referee who has special skills and independent judgment, and a masiador or sentenciador who had expertise in cockfight gambling.'
notable_anecdotes.purpose: Preserves the doctrinal taxonomy of who counts as a genuinely independent contractor -- and shows why riders do not.

notable_anecdotes.description: The Inquirer editorial labeled the decision a 'game-changing ruling for workers' -- a label that CJ Panganiban quotes approvingly.
notable_anecdotes.purpose: External editorial validation amplifying the column's activist-streak framing.

notable_anecdotes.description: The Court's closing dictum on security of tenure: 'When a person has no property, his job may possibly be his only possession or means of livelihood. Therefore, he should be protected against any arbitrary deprivation of his job' -- CJ adds, 'if I may say so myself, is reminiscent of my own philosophy of liberty and prosperity under the rule of law.'
notable_anecdotes.purpose: Personal-philosophical claim of lineage between Court doctrine and CJ's own FLP framework.

one_paragraph_summary: Even though the media had already reported it, CJ Panganiban gives Ditiangkin v. Lazada (Sept. 21, 2022; uploaded Jan. 19, 2023; Second Division, penned by SAJ Marvic M.V.F. Leonen with JJ Lazaro-Javier, Jhosep Lopez, and Kho Jr. concurring, J Mario Lopez on official business) a lookback because the Supreme Court 'once more demonstrated its activist and libertarian streak' by going beyond two sets of normal rules. The first set concerns appellate procedure: the SC normally dismisses Rule 45 petitions through the unsigned-resolution '1-2-3 rule' when the CA has affirmed the NLRC and the labor arbiter, and it normally refuses to review facts. In Lazada, the Court did the opposite -- waded deep into an exhaustive factual review and overturned the unanimous lower-tribunal finding that the riders were independent contractors. The second set concerns substantive labor classification: under the four-fold test (selection/engagement, wages, dismissal power, control -- with control 'the most significant factor'), Lazada failed to discharge its burden of showing the riders were not regular employees. The Court rejected the independent-contractor framing because the riders neither carried on 'a distinct and independent business' nor possessed the 'unique skills and talents' that distinguish the genuinely independent service class -- canonically the columnist, the basketball referee, and the masiador/sentenciador of cockfighting -- since 'picking up and delivering goods from warehouse to buyers does not call for specific expertise.' The constitutional anchor is the full-protection-to-labor clause and the corollary that 'when a person has no property, his job may possibly be his only possession or means of livelihood' so 'he should be protected against any arbitrary deprivation of his job' -- a closing dictum CJ explicitly recognizes as 'reminiscent of my own philosophy of liberty and prosperity under the rule of law.' The Inquirer editorial called it a 'game-changing ruling for workers'; CJ quotes the label approvingly.
